report.source_text:
Immediate treatment with calcium gluconate and magnesium sulphate intravenously was given in the emergency department while monitoring the patient’s heart. Quickly after administration of calcium, his voice improved.
We admitted the patient to the acute care unit where he continued to receive calcium intravenously together with alphacalcidol (1 μg) since his blood test showed hypoparathyroidism and cholecalciferol orally to restore his vitamin D concentration. After 24 hours, he received 20 mmol calcium in total, which resulted in plasma calcium of 1.57 mmol/L (reference range: 2.20–2.65 mmol/L) and a normal QTc interval. He was transferred to the hospital ward where he continued to receive calcium (10 mmol/24 hours) intravenously and alphacalcidol (1 ug) orally. After 5 days, his plasma calcium normalised (2.15 mmol/L) together with normalisation of his creatine kinase level, and he was discharged.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 29-year-old man presented with 3 months of progressive symptomatic hypocalcemia manifesting as laryngospasm (episodic speechlessness and hoarseness 8x/day lasting 30-40 seconds with dyspnea), esophageal spasm (vomiting after swallowing cold water), and tetany (hand spasms/cramps during driving, positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs). Initial laboratory evaluation revealed severe hypocalcemia (total calcium 1.03 mmol/L, reference 2.2-2.6) with normal albumin, hyperphosphatemia (2.21 mmol/L, reference 0.70-1.40), hypomagnesemia (0.58 mmol/L, reference 0.7-1.0), and markedly elevated CK (2962 IU/L, reference <170) consistent with rhabdomyolysis from muscle spasms. ECG demonstrated prolonged QTc interval (501 ms). Parathyroid hormone was inappropriately low at 0.7 pmol/L (reference 2-7) despite severe hypocalcemia, confirming primary hypoparathyroidism. Etiological workup revealed no mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) and no parathyroid antibodies, supporting the classification as idiopathic. The patient was treated with intravenous calcium gluconate and magnesium sulphate in the emergency department, with immediate improvement in voice symptoms. He received continued intravenous calcium (20 mmol total in 24 hours) combined with alphacalcidol (1 μg) and oral cholecalciferol, resulting in calcium normalization to 1.57 mmol/L with normalized QTc interval after 24 hours, and further normalization to 2.15 mmol/L with normalized CK after 5 days, at which point he was discharged on oral calcium and alphacalcidol.
